articles.title: Transparency and Responsibility Attribution: A Field Experiment in Western Uganda
articles.authors: Bill Schultz, Eric A. Coleman, Rani Parker, Jacob Manyindo, Emmanuel Mukuru
articles.abstract: The implementation of public policy is increasingly diffuse with responsibilities divided among several levels of government administration, the private sector, and nonprofits. In the face of such diffusion, many advocate for transparency initiatives to inform the public about policymaking. However, it remains unclear whether transparency initiatives clarify the blame and credit for policy, or what this means for collective action and accountability. Such concerns are especially pressing in complex settings like the non‐renewable extractives sector (oil, mining, and natural gas). We assess policy attributions of blame and credit using data from a field experiment that randomizes stakeholder engagement in Western Uganda's oil sector, building on our prior work showing that this intervention increased collective action. While participating in multistakeholder forums improved transparency for communities, we find that it did not change their attributions. In other words, improving transparency does not ensure that citizens will update their opinions about who is to blame for the problems they face. Yet, this did not preclude greater collective action. Evidence from this intervention highlights the need for more exploration of pathways linking transparency, collective action, and accountability.

articles.title: The Effects of Policy Success Versus Failure Narratives
articles.abstract: While public policies usually have mixed effects, succeeding at some aspects and failing at others, this nuance is often lost in public discourse when political actors like advocacy groups and politicians strategically emphasize either the successes or failures of particular policies. For example, advocacy groups often emphasize the failures of existing policy with the goal of galvanizing public attention and concern. However, little empirical evidence exists assessing the actual causal impact of these different approaches on public attitudes. This paper presents the results of a pre‐registered experiment in which participants watch a TikTok‐style short news video about either the success or failure of one of three different public policies and then are asked about their trust in government to handle the issue, their perceptions of the issue's importance, and their feelings of collective efficacy. While success and failure narratives are both effective at raising an issue's salience, focusing on a policy's failure has the downstream effect of increasing cynicism about the government's ability to address the issue.

articles.title: It Does Matter. A New Framework on the Influence of Policy Evaluation
articles.abstract: Governments worldwide have invested heavily in policy evaluation, providing many policymakers with a steady stream of evidence into the effectiveness, efficiency, or relevance of policies. Yet, despite these investments, systematic knowledge about the actual influence of policy evaluations remains surprisingly limited. This is partly due to the insufficient conceptual differentiation of policy evaluation as a distinct type of policy advice. Building on interdisciplinary evaluation literature and public policy scholarship, the article introduces a new framework designed to enhance our understanding and categorization of the changes policy evaluations bring about in terms of policy, polity, and politics, and how these dimensions interrelate. As a parsimonious heuristic tool, the framework enables a dynamic and comprehensive assessment of the influence of policy evaluations. It contributes to the theorization of policy evaluation influence and offers insights that may inform related research on the influence of expert knowledge, policy advice, and evidence‐informed policymaking more broadly.

articles.title: The Impact of National Pride and Migrant Occupational Status on Attitudes Toward Settlement-Oriented Emigration: Evidence From a Survey Experiment in China
articles.abstract: While migration studies have examined host-society attitudes toward immigrants, home-country views of emigrants remain underexplored. We address this gap using an online survey experiment in China that varies (i) the salience of national pride and (ii) the prospective emigrant's occupational status. Making national pride salient lowers support for — and increases negative emotional reactions toward — settlement-oriented emigration, especially for lower- and mid-skill profiles; effects for the high-status profile are smaller and statistically uncertain. Net of the prime, attitudes are also more negative toward higher-status profiles than toward the low-skill profile. We interpret these patterns within a social identity framework, drawing on Social Identity Theory, the “brain drain” literature, and Hirschman's exit–voice–loyalty model, while emphasizing a mechanism of identity salience consistent with Self-Categorization Theory. The study advances international migration scholarship by showing how national identity and occupational status shape home-country evaluations of settlement-oriented emigration and by foregrounding emotions as a mechanism linking identity salience to policy-relevant attitudes.

articles.title: Book Review: Age and Immigration Policy in Canada Clark-KazakChristina. 2026. Age and Immigration Policy in Canada: Toward an Equitable Approach. Vancouver: UBC Press. 198 pages. £29.99(Open Access Edition available).
Analyzing Online Migration Forums: An Introduction to Natural Language Processing for International Migration Research
articles.authors: Nari Yoo, Donghun Kim, Sou Hyun Jang, Eric Fong
articles.abstract: In contemporary migration studies, online forums are common spaces where people exchange information and seek advice about international migration. This methods note introduces the Reddit community r/IWantOut as a data source for studying migration aspirations and presents a validated natural language processing (NLP) pipeline for analyzing it. The forum's community rules require posters to encode age, gender, origin, and intended destinations in a fixed title format, so users label their own migration aspirations in a semi-machine-readable form when they post. Using 156,313 submissions from 2009 to 2026 (58,892 after cleaning), we demonstrate three analytical approaches: (1) time-series analysis to identify temporal shifts in discourse volume, (2) dictionary- and rule-based extraction, together with Named Entity Recognition (NER), to recover origin–destination pairs and sociodemographic attributes from the structured titles, and (3) large language model (LLM)-based zero-shot classification, used only for classifying migration motivations. Validation against human-coded labels across three LLMs (GPT-4.1, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, and DeepSeek-V3) showed that GPT-4.1 achieved the highest agreement (mean κ = 0.566), with substantial agreement on push factors, moderate agreement on pull and enabling factors, and fair agreement on constraining factors. Applying this approach to 56,242 international migration posts, we found that enabling factors (individual-level resources) appeared most frequently (77.3%), followed by constraining factors (49.3%), pull factors (37.2%), and push factors (23.6%). For each method, we provide practical guidance on implementation, data access, and validation, and reflect on methodological limitations and ethical considerations.

articles.title: Who Governs Migrant Precarity? Intermediated Exclusion Under Conditions of Intensified Vulnerability
articles.abstract: Who governs migrant precarity, and through what mechanisms is it sustained in contemporary labor migration regimes? This article conceptualizes intermediated exclusion as a governance logic through which accountability is displaced, producing migrant precarity. Drawing on a nationwide employer survey (n = 3,747) and qualitative evidence from labor brokers, local officials, and migrant workers in Taiwan, it identifies three modes of delegated governance: institutional outsourcing, household-level ambiguity, and hybrid flexibility. These arrangements shift responsibility away from the state, embedding precarity through wage opacity, dependence on brokers, and the policing of ‘runaway’ cases. The article shows that delegated governance not only fails to protect migrant workers, but also contributes to the organization of vulnerability through dispersed forms of authority. Beyond Taiwan, the findings suggest that migrant precarity is less an exception than a patterned outcome of how labor migration governance is enacted in practice.

articles.title: How do people view income inequality in China? An interactive framework of inequality and economic growth
articles.abstract: Economic inequality has become a pressing societal challenge worldwide, yet less is known about how individuals perceive and evaluate it. Drawing on longitudinal data from the China Family Panel Studies (CFPS 2012–2018), this study uses modified hierarchical linear models to examine how objective inequality interacts with economic growth in shaping subjective inequality. The results show, first, that the average association between objective inequality and respondents’ severity ratings of inequality (SRI) is weak and not statistically significant. Second, economic growth moderates this association: objective inequality is associated with higher SRI only under low-growth conditions. Finally, this moderating role of economic growth is salient only among socio-economically disadvantaged individuals. These findings enhance our understanding of how individuals view economic inequality in China’s post-high-speed growth era and provide broader comparative implications for societies characterized by different configurations of inequality and economic growth.

Online gendered violence and visibility in electoral autocracies: Evidence from multi-level elections in Türkiye
articles.authors: Jungmin Han, Müge Finkel, Steven Finkel, Firat Duruşan, Erdem Yörük
articles.abstract: Online platforms have become indispensable tools for political candidates to gain visibility, particularly for female candidates in electoral autocracies who often lack access to traditional networks, party hierarchies, and media platforms. We argue that online visibility, while a resource for female candidates, disproportionately exposes them to online violence that functions as a mechanism of political control, reinforcing patriarchal exclusion from the political sphere. Our analysis draws on more than three million tweets directed at 1,834 candidates across the 2023 parliamentary and 2024 local election campaigns in Türkiye, providing a rare opportunity to observe how these dynamics unfold at both the national and subnational levels. We find that while online visibility increases abuse for all candidates, the effect is markedly stronger for female candidates, who are disproportionately targeted across diverse forms of violence, including profanity, demeaning and ridiculing language, physical threats, and ethnic and religious hate speech. Moreover, our results suggest that in local elections, where candidates rely more heavily on personalized campaigns, increases in visibility are more strongly associated with female candidates’ exposure to online violence.

articles.title: Losing elections, losing trust? A quasi-experimental investigation of the winner-loser gap on political trust
articles.abstract: Voters’ experiences of winning or losing elections significantly influence their attitudes, particularly satisfaction with democracy, while other outcomes such as trust are less studied. Additionally, studies often rely on observational data, limiting causal conclusions about effects. We make three key contributions to this literature. First, we use a quasi-experimental design based on the implementation of the European Quality of Government Index Survey during elections across several European countries and regions to demonstrate causal effects of elections on trust. Second, we introduce a novel theoretical argument that voters of populist parties are especially sensitive to electoral outcomes. Third, we explore three ways to define ‘winners’ and ‘losers’: government/opposition status, vote margin changes, and results relative to recent polling. Our findings show that elections generally boost trust, with a pronounced winner-loser gap driven by winners, particularly when measured as entering government. Additionally, populist party voters exhibit greater sensitivity to these effects.

articles.title: Preferences or principles? The ‘noncompliance penalty’ and the limits of public support for the rule of law
articles.authors: Taylor Kinsley Chewning, Amanda Driscoll, Martín Gandur, Jay N. Krehbiel, Michael J. Nelson
articles.abstract: When will individuals support government noncompliance with the written law? A bedrock principle of the rule of law is that politicians who fail to comply with written law will face political consequences. Drawing on survey experiments fielded in two consolidated democracies, we introduce the noncompliance penalty , the loss of public support for a government action that contravenes the law. The results show that citizens do penalize governmental noncompliance with the law. However, we find that this penalty decreases if government noncompliance advances the policy interests of favored protest groups, and mixed evidence that this penalty increases with professed support for the rule of law. Perhaps surprisingly, our results suggest that citizens with the strongest commitment to the rule of law can become the most accepting of noncompliance if it advances their policy goals. These findings have important implications for understanding whether the public will punish politicians who disregard the formal letter of the law.

articles.title: Power, politics, and policy agency: towards a Functional Theory of Agency
articles.authors: Oliver Meza, Ana Cecilia de Alba
articles.abstract: This article examines how political position shapes policy agency in local policy making. Specifically, it asks: what patterns of policy agency functions do municipal councillors ( regidores ) exhibit in the local policy process? Drawing on the Functional Theory of Agency framework and a sequential mixed-methods design combining a national survey of Mexican municipal councillors with follow-up semi-structured interviews, we analyse how councillors exercise four modes of policy agency: steering, innovation, intermediation, and intelligence. Our findings reveal systematic differences between majoritarian and opposition councillors. Majoritarian councillors dominate commissions, align with mayoral priorities, and primarily act as steerers and brokers of executive policy. By contrast, opposition councillors, who are often excluded from formal decision-making arenas, engage in disruptive innovation, cultivate vertical alliances beyond the municipality, and invest more heavily in knowledge production as a counter-power strategy. These distinct patterns suggest that political position shapes the policy agency functions available to local legislators and influences how they seek to affect policy outcomes. The article contributes to the consolidation of a Functional Theory of Agency by demonstrating how unequal access to formal policy-making authority structures actors’ behavioural repertoires within policy-making processes. It also advances comparative research on legislative actors by showing how local representatives adapt their policy agency strategies under conditions of unequal access to formal policy-making authority.

articles.title: The Leadership Premium: Committee Leadership Status and Political Donations to Incumbent Legislators in South Korea
articles.abstract: This study investigates the effect of committee leadership positions on political fundraising in the South Korean National Assembly from 2004 to 2019. Drawing upon theories of legislative power and campaign finance, we examine whether acquiring standing committee chairmanships significantly increases political contributions received by legislators, even within Korea's highly restrictive regulatory regime that prohibits corporate donations. Utilizing OLS regression and difference‐in‐differences with Panel Matching methodology, we find compelling evidence of a substantial leadership premium. OLS estimates reveal that committee chairs consistently outraise non‐chairs by 16%–21%; Panel Matching estimates confirm an immediate increase of approximately 1.15 log‐points (a 216% increase) following chair appointment. Event study analysis validates our identification strategy by demonstrating parallel pre‐trends and sharp treatment effects at the moment of leadership transition, with effects dissipating after chairs leave their positions. Split‐sample OLS estimates reveal a cross‐over pattern: the premium is significant for Targeted and Mixed committees in the first half of the legislative term but shifts to Universal committees in the second half, suggesting that the relevant dimension of heterogeneity may be whether a committee holds jurisdictional authority over concentrated regulatory or budgetary stakes. These findings demonstrate that the link between institutional power and political money persists even under highly restrictive campaign finance regimes—reflecting structural features of legislative organization that transcend specific regulatory designs. The individual‐as‐proxy mechanism we identify, whereby organized interest groups circumvent the corporate donation ban through coordinated individual‐level contributions, suggests that regulation reshapes the channels of strategic giving without eliminating its underlying demand.

articles.title: The Emerging Market for Intelligence: How Firms Buy and Sell AI
articles.authors: Mert Demirer, Andrey Fradkin, Nadav Tadelis
articles.abstract: We describe the emerging business-to-business market for large language model (LLM) inference and document key empirical patterns in its supply, pricing, and dynamics, using data from OpenRouter. First, supply has expanded rapidly: the number of commercially available models, model creators, and inference providers has grown sharply, driven heavily by opensource entrants. Second, the price of intelligence has fallen roughly a thousandfold, and opensource models now cost about 90 percent less than comparable closed-source ones. Third, the market is highly dynamic, with frequent turnover among leading models and creators. Fourth, we document substantial horizontal and vertical differentiation: no single model dominates across use cases, and demand for intelligence varies widely across applications. We place these patterns in historical perspective alongside earlier general-purpose technologies.

articles.title: Should We Tax Trade? A Pigouvian Perspective
articles.abstract: We develop a simple and intuitive Pigouvian perspective on optimal trade policy. Our approach unifies a wide range of rationales for taxing trade, from the classical optimal tariff argument to contemporary debates about global carbon emissions and geopolitics. We also clarify when trade policy intervention is warranted and when alternative domestic instruments should be used instead.

articles.title: US Tariff Policy Since 1789
articles.authors: Miguel Acosta, Lydia Cox, Andrew Greenland, John Lopresti, Christopher M. Meissner, Martin Rotemberg, Sharon Traiberman
articles.abstract: We use a newly assembled, tariff-line-level dataset spanning the full history of US trade policy to revisit the evolution of tariffs since 1789. We document the institutional shift from Congressional setting to multilateral negotiation, the steady growth in granularity of the tariff code alongside expanding administrative capacity, and the under-appreciated role of specific tariffs, which feature prominently throughout US history and whose ad valorem equivalent moves mechanically with prices. We discuss the implications of this relationship for how we interpret past liberalization episodes and for empirical identification of tariff effects. Finally, we outline how the new data can advance research on the political economy of tariff-setting and on the macroeconomic and distributional consequences of trade policy.

articles.title: Leniency Designs: An Operator's Manual
articles.authors: Paul Goldsmith-Pinkham, Peter Hull, Michal Kolesár
articles.abstract: We develop a step-by-step guide to leniency (a.k.a. judge or examiner instrument) designs, drawing on recent econometric literatures. The unbiased jackknife instrumental variables estimator (UJIVE) is purpose-built for leveraging exogenous leniency variation, avoiding subtle biases even in the presence of many decision-makers or controls. We show how UJIVE can also be used to assess key assumptions underlying leniency designs, including quasi-random assignment and average first-stage monotonicity, and to probe the external validity of treatment effect estimates. We further discuss statistical inference, arguing that non-clustered standard errors are often appropriate. A reanalysis of Farre-Mensa et al. (2020), using quasi-random examiner assignment to estimate the value of patents to startups, illustrates our checklist.

articles.title: Stefanie Stantcheva, 2025 Clark Medalist
articles.abstract: The American Economic Association awarded the 2025 John Bates Clark Medal to Stefanie Stantcheva of Harvard University. Her research ranges widely in the field of public economic. It includes theoretical contributions to optimal income taxation, empirical contributions to the study of how income tax rates across countries and states affect the mobility of inventors and the level of innovation, and contributions in the development and execution of on-line surveys to measure respondents' beliefs about economic primitives, such as the distribution of income or the rate of inflation, and the way these beliefs influence policy preferences. She has demonstrated that randomized controlled trials can be embedded within on-line surveys and used to the way informational interventions and other treatments affect economic beliefs and policy preferences.

articles.title: Evaluating the Fiscal and Distributional Implications of Tariffs
articles.abstract: The Trump administration has enacted a series of significant taxes on imports, including an across-the-board tariff on nearly all imports. Tariffs are now expected to raise nearly 1 percent of GDP in revenue. Given tariffs' growing importance as a source of revenue, it is important to understand their implications for federal finances and the wellbeing of households. This paper describes and reviews current revenue and distributional analyses of tariffs.

articles.title: Recommendations for Further Reading
Correct (and Incorrect) Inference with a Single Instrumental Variable: Practical Takeaways from the Weak Instruments Literature
articles.abstract: Most empirical economists have encountered the warning that instrumental variables can be “weak,” but the underlying issues—what makes an instrument weak, why weakness distorts inference, and what to do about it—are less widely understood. This article offers an accessible introduction to the weak instruments problem for the common just-identified case of a single endogenous regressor and a single instrument. We explain why the usual two-stage least squares t-ratio and its “±1.96 times the standard error” confidence interval can yield incorrect inferences, much as homoskedasticity-only standard errors do when errors are not homoskedastic. We then describe practical, robust-to-weak-instrument solutions—including the Anderson-Rubin and tF methods—that deliver valid confidence intervals whatever the instrument's true strength, and we offer some do's and don'ts, notably why the popular “F greater than 10” rule has no theoretical justification in this setting.

articles.title: Global Imbalances, Tariffs, and Industrial Policy
articles.authors: Pierre-Olivier Gourinchas, Gene Kindberg-Hanlon, Manasa Patnam, Lorenzo Rotunno, Michele Ruta
articles.abstract: Global imbalances denote the distribution of countries' current account balances, identically equal to the difference between two forward-looking aggregate variables: national saving and domestic investment. Industrial and trade policies have traditionally not been considered important drivers of aggregate saving or investment, and therefore of current account balances. The former because most industrial policies are small in scope; the latter because permanent tariffs have no intertemporal effect in the textbook model, with an offsetting appreciation of the real exchange rate. The rapidly growing use of both industrial and trade policies in recent years calls for a reassessment. This paper presents a framework to think about the role of both policies. For industrial policy, we make the important distinction between the traditional sector-specific policies via subsidies or other targeted instruments (“micro industrial policy”) and broader policies (“macro industrial policy”) that aim to promote industrial developments and competitiveness through the deployment of more aggregate instruments such as financial repression, foreign reserve accumulation, or capital controls. A key finding is that micro industrial policy tends to increase external balances if it fails to raise aggregate productivity. By contrast, macro industrial policy can, under some conditions, boost the current account, forcing other countries to adjust. Yet, these policies often come at the cost of suppressed domestic consumption and possibly domestic welfare. Our analysis confirms that tariffs are a weak tool to improve current account balances. Finally, traditional macroeconomic drivers—such as fiscal policy, demographics or credit cycles—remain critical drivers of global imbalances, especially for the United States and China.

articles.title: AI and Our Economic Future
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) will likely be the most transformative technology of the modern era. What if machines—AI for cognitive tasks and AI plus advanced robots for physical tasks—can perform every task a human can? This essay makes three main points. First, even though US growth rates have been stable at roughly 2 percent per year for 150 years, it is distinctly possible that automating intelligence leads economic growth rates to accelerate. Second, this acceleration is likely to be slowed by the presence of “weak links.” While we each have access to 100 million times more transistors on our desktop computer than people in the 1970s, we are not 100 million times more productive. Computers can invert matrices at lightning speed, but we humans must still decide what matrix to invert, what hypothesis to test, and so on. Accelerating economic growth requires the vast majority of the weak links to be automated away, which delays the large gains. Finally, even though weak links slow the benefits, they may actually speed up the risks. When a chain is only as strong as its weakest link, damaging one link in the chain can be very costly. A powerful AI that is superhuman at software engineering could be misused by a bad actor to do substantial harm by hacking the financial system or a virology lab.

articles.title: Labor Market Responses to Tariffs: Frictions, Dynamics, and Policy Responses
articles.abstract: This article introduces the evidence and associated modeling frameworks contemporary economists use to understand the effects of trade and trade policy on labor markets, with a particular emphasis on labor-market frictions and adjustment dynamics. The effects of trade shocks differ across industries, regions, and occupations, implying the presence of important adjustment frictions in labor markets, and these effects evolve slowly over time, implying the need for dynamic frameworks rationalizing slow transitions. After reviewing the key insights from this literature, we discuss policies aimed at mitigating costs to workers and ensuring that the gains from trade are shared more equitably.

articles.title: The Incidence of Tariffs: Rates and Reality
articles.abstract: In 2025, statutory tariff rates on US imports rose to levels not seen in over one hundred years. What were the implications for prices? On the one hand, shipping lags, exemptions, and enforcement gaps kept the actual implemented rates at only half of the statutory rates, moderating the tariffs' impact. On the other hand, tariff pass-through to US import prices reached 92 percent, so the United States bore a large share of the costs. We study the incidence of the 2018-2019 and 2025 US tariffs and discuss implications for US sourcing, domestic manufacturing costs, and the dollar.

articles.title: Senior Bureaucrats, Coalitions and the Quality of Government: Accounting for Effective Governance in Fragmented Settings
articles.abstract: Debates over the consequences of party and cabinet fragmentation for government performance remain unsettled. While some scholars argue that coalition governments foster instability and rent‐seeking, others contend that they enhance accountability and inclusion. This article argues that the effects of cabinet fragmentation depend on the rules of recruitment and promotion of the senior civil service. Using data from the Quality of Government Expert Survey covering 89 democracies, we examine how fragmentation interacts with both bureaucratic politicization and bureaucratic career systems. The results show that fragmentation amplifies the negative effects of politicized senior appointments, although we find limited evidence that fragmentation itself reduces the quality of government under high politicization. By contrast, fragmented cabinets are associated with more effective governance in the presence of career‐based structures characterized by internal recruitment of senior bureaucrats and long‐term careers. The findings highlight the importance of bureaucratic career structures for effective governance in multiparty systems.

Let Them Eat Pie: Addressing Sample Selection in Multiparty Elections
articles.authors: Ali Kagalwala, Thiago M. Q. Moreira, Guy D. Whitten, Yongzhi Xu
articles.abstract: Elections are central to the study of politics. When studying parties’ vote shares across districts, scholars are encouraged to use compositional-outcome models in order to test their theories about what factors shape the dynamics of electoral support. Existing compositional modeling approaches incorrectly deal with scenarios in which not all parties compete in every electoral district. Because unobserved factors that affect a party’s decisions to contest a district are likely correlated with its performance in districts where the party fielded candidates, failing to account for partial contestation is likely to result in sample selection bias. Addressing sample selection in a compositional setting is challenging because the outcomes are in log-ratio form, and thus the errors often deviate from normality. To deal with these issues, we introduce a novel maximum likelihood approach which accounts for this type of sample selection and demonstrate through simulations that our method outperforms commonly used solutions, including the conventional Heckman correction. We illustrate the utility of our approach by analyzing the 2017 and 2019 U.K. parliamentary elections in English constituencies.

articles.title: The Power of Prognosis: Improving Covariate Balance Tests with Outcome Information
articles.authors: Clara Bicalho, Adam Bouyamourn, Thad Dunning
articles.abstract: Scholars frequently use covariate balance tests to test the validity of natural experiments and related designs. Unfortunately, when measured covariates are unrelated to potential outcomes, balance is uninformative about key identification conditions. We show that balance tests can then lead to erroneous conclusions. To build stronger tests, researchers should identify covariates that are jointly predictive of potential outcomes; formally measure and report covariate prognosis; and prioritize the most individually informative variables in tests. Building on prior research on “prognostic scores,” we develop bootstrap balance tests that upweight covariates associated with the outcome. We adapt this approach for regression-discontinuity designs and use simulations to compare weighting methods based on linear regression and more flexible methods, including machine learning. The results show how prognosis weighting can avoid both false negatives and false positives. To illustrate key points, we study empirical examples from a sample of published studies, including an important debate over close elections.

articles.title: Reproductive Rights, Reframed: Federalism and Vote Choice in the 2024 Election
articles.authors: Spencer Goidel, Joseph A. Aistrup, John C. Morris, Martin K. Mayer, R. Bruce Anderson, Robert C. Kenter
articles.abstract: The overturning of Roe v. Wade sent shockwaves through the American political system. Running on women’s reproductive health care rights, Democrats vastly outperformed expectations in the 2022 midterm elections. The 2024 US presidential election provided a test of whether broad public support for reproductive health care access would continue to translate into electoral gains for Democrats. Using a novel set of survey questions, this article examines attitudes toward abortion and the abortion pill (i.e., mifepristone) as well as preferences over whether policy should be decided federally or by individual states (i.e., locus of authority). Our findings provide partial support for the expectation that locus-of-authority preferences shape vote choice. Whereas support for a constitutional protection for abortion remained strongly associated with voting against Trump regardless of locus-of-authority preferences, the pattern for mifepristone access more closely matched our expectations. Among voters who supported mifepristone access, those who were comfortable leaving the issue to the states were significantly more likely to support Donald Trump. His emphasis on state control may have functioned as strategic ambiguity, especially on a less-polarized reproductive health issue such as mifepristone access.

articles.title: Teaching Election Inversions in the Electoral College: Two Simple Models
articles.abstract: The Electoral College is an important concept in many undergraduate American politics courses. Although students often understand the basics of the “House-seats-plus-two” rule and the “winner-take-all” system, many struggle to understand election inversions, in which the winner of the popular vote loses the Electoral College vote and therefore loses the presidency. This article presents two models using only foundational arithmetic to explain election inversions, including an example illustrating how a Republican candidate could also win the popular vote but lose the Electoral College vote. A survey of student-learning experiences showed positive results: students found the models accessible and helpful, and they reported greater confidence in the integrity of US presidential elections and in American democracy after working with the materials. These models can be incorporated into a range of American politics courses to help even first-year undergraduate students make sense of the US presidential election system.

articles.title: Democracy for Whom? Herrenvolk Democracy and the American Founding
articles.abstract: As the United States marks the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence amid democratic erosion, this article asks why 250 years of democratic development have not produced a multiracial democracy. It argues that the United States is a herrenvolk democracy—a regime in which democracy coexists with racialized limits on political membership and governing power. By examining colonial law, the Declaration, the Constitution, and the Naturalization Act of 1790, I show how the founding joined popular sovereignty to racial exclusion in ways that continue to shape struggles over belonging, representation, and coercive power. The legacy of 1776 includes both the Declaration’s democratic promise and a durable model for how democracy can coexist with exclusion.

content.journal_name: Journal of Public Administration Research and Theory

articles.title: Large Language Models and Conversational Counter-Arguments to Anti-Public Sector Bias
articles.authors: John D Marvel, Sheeling Neo, Rachel Cho, Sangwon Ju
articles.abstract: Can a good argument change an individual’s mind? In three pre-registered experiments, we explore this question in the domain of public sector organizational performance. We observe human subjects as they engage in conversations with a generative artificial intelligence (AI) programmed to argue in one of seven distinct “styles,” including a confrontational challenger style, a didactic style, and a sycophantic style. We develop a theory of effective argumentation predicting that conversational styles which are pleasant and engaging will be more persuasive than styles which are unpleasant or unstimulating. Contrary to this prediction, we find that conversational styles which challenge subjects’ negative views of government agencies produce significant positive attitude change, while sycophantic styles that indulge those views do not. Troublingly, subjects find the sycophantic styles more enjoyable, less frustrating, and more credible than the challenger styles. This dissociation between user experience and persuasive outcome—what we call “grudging persuasion”—suggests that attitude change does not require a pleasant conversational experience, and that the styles subjects enjoy most may be precisely the ones least likely to move them. Our findings point to a potentially dark side of LLM-based persuasion: sycophantic styles that users find most appealing are the least effective at correcting misinformed views.

articles.title: The Knowledge Gap in a High-Choice Media Environment: Experimental Evidence from Online Search
articles.authors: Roberto Ulloa, Leonard Tiedemann, Peter Selb, Celina Kacperski

articles.title: I or We? Linked Fate, Self-Interest, and African American Opinion Toward Reparations
articles.authors: Tatishe M. Nteta, Jesse H. Rhodes, Bel Corder, Seth K. Goldman, Yuen J. Huo, Efrén Pérez, Linda R. Tropp
articles.abstract: Recent years have witnessed renewed calls for reparations to advance racial equality in the United States. In response, a number of localities and institutions of higher education have provided reparations to the descendants of slaves. However, the policy remains controversial as evidenced by a clear racial divide characterized by overwhelmingly White opposition to reparations and strong majorities of African Americans supporting the provision of cash payments to the descendants of slaves. While much attention has been paid to empirical explorations of White opinion, in this paper we investigate the determinants of African American opinion, with a particular focus on the influence of measures of economic self-interest and linked fate in structuring African American opinion. Using data from two large national surveys of Americans, we find consistent evidence that linked fate is a strong and consistent predictor of African American support for reparations, while self-interest is a weaker and less consistent predictor, controlling for a wide array of political, socioeconomic, and attitudinal factors. These findings are reinforced by quantitative and qualitative content analysis of open-ended responses by African Americans to the question why they support reparations. Our results suggest that African Americans’ views on reparations are more strongly associated with the well-being of the African American community and less to do with the individual economic benefits of the policy.

articles.title: Belief and Betrayal: Institutional Trust in the Shadow of Religious Violence
articles.authors: Tang Xi, Chang Li, Kalsoom Paracha, Shaukat Hussain Bhatti
articles.abstract: Religious violence erodes the moral and social fabric that binds communities, striking at the very heart of societal cohesion. As fear and intolerance spread, the foundations of institutional trust weaken, leaving nations vulnerable to deep-seated divisions and governance challenges. Present investigation analyzes the asymmetric impact of religious violence on institutional trust in 10 selected emerging countries (India, Indonesia, Pakistan, Nigeria, Egypt, Brazil, Turkey, South Africa, Mexico, and the Philippines). Departing from conventional analyses that rely on standard econometric techniques and often overlook regional heterogeneity, the present investigation uses the cutting-edge Quantile-on-Quantile method. This approach facilitates a nuanced examination of cross-country variation, enhances analytical precision, and reveals intricate, nation-specific behavioral dynamics. The results exhibit a strong negative association between religious violence and institutional trust in most sample countries. In contrast, South Africa and Mexico exhibit a mixed association. These findings underscore notable variations across quantiles, highlighting the asymmetric nature of the relationship between the variables. They emphasize that policymakers must undertake thorough assessments and formulate strategies tailored to each country’s specific social and regional contexts, ensuring that the multifaceted and sensitive link between religious violence and institutional trust is addressed effectively and in a locally responsive manner.

Party membership motivations and political activism in a polarized new democracy: Evidence from South Korea
articles.abstract: This study investigates party membership motivations in South Korea, a highly polarized new democracy, and how they distinctively shape intra-party and campaign participation. Using survey data from 1,410 Democratic and People Power Party members, we evaluate the General Incentives Model alongside negative partisan motivation. Results show that while altruism is the primary reason for joining, higher affective polarization significantly intensifies negative partisan motivation, making it a key membership driver, particularly among conservatives. Crucially, engagement mechanisms are not monolithic: selective benefits predict both forms of participation, whereas collective policy motives specifically foster campaigning. Conversely, social norms motivation deters visible campaigning due to polarization-induced cross-pressures. Furthermore, negative partisan motivation reduces routine intra-party engagement without increasing campaign involvement. Ultimately, membership surges driven by out-group hostility produce “detached members,” indicating that expanding party rolls in polarized contexts does not automatically deepen democratic participation or organizational capacity.

articles.title: Ethno-regionalist parties beyond Western Europe: Kurdish parties in Turkey
articles.abstract: While there is an extensive literature on ethno-regionalist parties (ERPs) in Western Europe, Kurdish ERPs in Turkey remain undertheorized. Focusing on party ideology, organizational structure, and electoral strategy, this article advances three findings. First, ideologically, Kurdish ERPs consistently articulate a left-leaning program centered on labor and democratization, while increasingly integrating post-materialist tenets such as feminism and environmentalism. Second, organizationally, they function as movement parties with a highly resilient structure. Third, strategically, they expand beyond their ethnic stronghold through broad leftist alliances and a “Turkification” ( Türkiyelileşme ) process, becoming pivotal national actors. These findings underscore the need to account for the interaction between ethno-regional mobilization, political-institutional constraints, and party-movement linkages in understanding ERPs in the European periphery.

articles.title: Ambition and access: Linking regional opportunity structures and career-ambitious youth party members
articles.authors: Clint Claessen, Stefanie Bailer, Tamaki Ohmura
articles.abstract: Youth party members are primarily driven by intrinsic moral and social motives, yet ambitions for political and professional careers vary considerably across individuals. Building on findings linking parties' national opportunity structures to having an increase in career-ambitious youth wing members, this research note examines opportunity structures at the regional level. Using a self-collected survey of youth party members in Germany (2017–2018, n = 1216), we show that career-ambitious members are particularly frequent in youth parties that are organizationally strong with numerous local and (sub)regional branches where ambitious youth wing members can make a career. Therefore, this research note provides a key insight into the motivations of young people, and especially those pursuing a political career, for joining youth parties and speaks to a broader literature concerned with political ambition, party organization, and careers.

articles.title: Carbon Pricing and Inflation Expectations
articles.authors: Michael D Bauer, Diego R Känzig, Glenn D Rudebusch
articles.abstract: Putting a price on carbon emissions helps mitigate climate change but may also raise overall price inflation. Using high-frequency event studies based on regulatory news in the European carbon market, we show that carbon price surprises generate significant increases not only in energy futures prices, but also in inflation swap rates and breakeven inflation rates. These measures of inflation compensation respond positively at both short and long horizons, with significant effects up to ten years out. Such persistent effects of climate policy on market-based inflation expectations are relevant for central banks. However, despite the sustained effects on inflation compensation, forward-looking nominal interest rates show no meaningful response to the carbon policy shocks, suggesting that investors do not anticipate that the European Central Bank will lean against the inflationary effects of higher carbon prices.

content.journal_name: British Journal of Politics & International Relations

articles.title: Risk mitigation versus gains maximisation – The two logics of smaller power hedging amid intensifying great power rivalry
articles.abstract: How can smaller powers use hedging effectively to navigate the intensifying great power rivalry? Why can some smaller powers hedge successfully between competing great powers while others fail and suffer serious harm? The burgeoning hedging literature is largely silent about which hedging patterns are likely to be more successful and why. This research contributes to the field by discerning and specifying two distinct modes of hedging – “risk mitigation” and “gains maximisation” – and their implications for hedging outcomes under intensifying great power rivalry. It argues that while these two modes might seem similar, and the extant literature has so far failed to separate them, primarily conceiving hedging as risk minimisation, they have different operational logics and are likely to have different consequences for the hedging states. It probes the two concepts using cases of smaller power hedging in Southeast Asia (Malaysia and Vietnam), exposed to the China–US rivalry, and in the post-Soviet space (Georgia and Ukraine), exposed to the Russia–North Atlantic Treaty Organization rivalry. It further argues that as great power rivalry intensifies, abandoning the gains maximisation and consolidating the risk-mitigation logic of hedging can help mitigate threats posed by great powers and minimise the chances of hedging failure.

articles.title: Party organisation and the strategic use of federal narratives in electoral campaigns: Evidence from Assam, India
articles.abstract: This article examines how party organisation shapes the construction of federal narratives during electoral competition, drawing on fieldwork from the 2024 parliamentary elections in Assam, India. Using interviews, campaign speeches, and party materials, it compares four parties across two constituencies, Dhubri and Guwahati: the Indian National Congress, the Bharatiya Janata Party, the Asom Gana Parishad, and the All-India United Democratic Front. The findings show that parties construct representations of their relationship with the Centre within campaign discourse. These vary systematically with organisational form and constituency context, particularly across settings shaped by citizenship anxieties and urban governance concerns. The article argues that federalism functions as a conditional rhetorical resource, highlighting how party communication in multi-level systems is shaped by organisational capacity and local political conditions.

The role of AI competencies: How do AI knowledge, skills, and attitudes shape users’ understanding and evaluation of explainable news recommendations?
articles.authors: Chenyue Wang, Anne C. Kroon, Judith Möller, Claes H. de Vreese, Sophie C. Boerman
articles.abstract: This study investigates how explanations in AI-driven news recommender systems (RS) influence user understanding, trust, and attitudes toward the RS, and whether these effects depend on individual differences in AI competence. An online experiment ( N = 754) was conducted in the Netherlands with a no-explanation condition as baseline. Results show that joint explanations significantly improved users’ objective understanding of the RS but had no consistent direct effects on perceived understanding, trust, or attitudes toward the RS. Exploratory structural equation modeling revealed an indirect pathway in which explanations enhanced objective understanding, which increased perceived understanding, subsequently fostering greater trust and more positive attitudes. Moderation analyses showed limited evidence for AI competence conditioning explanation effects, with small benefits concentrated among users with higher AI knowledge. Together, these findings suggest that explanations in news RS are not universally effective: their effects appear to operate primarily through cognitive mechanisms, while competence-related differences remain limited and selective.

articles.title: Algorithmic muteness: How algorithmic management obstructs platform content operators’ resonance with their labor
articles.authors: Zhenyu Qiu, Jinfeng Du, Irina Y. Yu, Jiankun Gong, Yu Zuo
articles.abstract: Workers who plan, curate, and promote content fuel platforms’ traffic success, yet frequently experience their labor as leaving no meaningful trace. While critical scholarship links this estrangement to algorithmic management, how it reshapes the quality of workers’ relationship with their own labor remains underexplored. Drawing on Rosa’s Resonance Theory and 27 interviews with platform content operators at China’s leading internet companies, this study reveals how algorithmic management obstructs resonance across content production, distribution, and feedback. Quantification hollows out labor’s normative worth; black-boxing forecloses self-efficacy through the (un)controllability paradox; amplification and acceleration suspend the possibility of self-transformation, even amid measurable success. We conceptualize ‘algorithmic muteness’, which captures a relational state—workers maintain high-intensity, data-mediated contact with their labor, yet this contact rarely yields genuine responsiveness. Algorithmic muteness moves beyond documenting the static, structural consequences of algorithmic management (e.g. alienation, meaninglessness) to tracing the relational process producing them, while critically revealing algorithms’ deep entanglement with platform capital.

articles.title: Do WhatsApp news channels help users navigate the information environment? A field experiment on information-related attitudes
articles.authors: Camila Mont’Alverne, Patrícia Rossini, Antonis Kalogeropoulos
articles.abstract: Messaging applications have become central sources of news, especially in the Global South, raising concerns about the quality of information circulating in these spaces. This study examines how receiving news through WhatsApp channels shapes key information-related attitudes in Brazil, including misinformation belief, news fatigue, and media trust. In a pre‑registered experiment conducted in November/December 2024, 601 participants from multiple Brazilian states were asked to subscribe to either a regional news channel or a fact‑checking channel operated by Globo, the largest media group in Latin America. The results show that accessing news via WhatsApp does not alter more stable attitudes, such as belief in misinformation or trust. However, it does reduce news fatigue and increases engagement with news on WhatsApp. As news consumption shifts toward private messaging platforms, these findings suggest their value lies less in reshaping political attitudes and more in maintaining routine connections between audiences and journalism.

articles.title: A Critical Geopolitics Analysis of “Critical Minerals” Discourses from Formal Geopolitics, Indigenous and Civil Society Actors
Differences in EU citizen voter registration: Evidence from French local elections
articles.abstract: The 1992 Maastricht Treaty guarantees European Union citizens the right to vote in local and European elections held in their country of residence. Yet, few mobile European Union citizens actually exercise this right. In France, which hosts the second-largest number of EU immigrants, only 26.2% of this population were registered to vote for the 2020 local elections. This article uses traditional explanations of immigrant electoral participation to understand the low electoral participation of foreign EU citizens. We combine census, electoral and local data to examine the determinants of registration rates for the nine largest EU nationalities in France. Our findings suggest that existing theories of resistance, transferability and exposure account for differences in electoral registration, while also suggesting that municipality size is an important factor.

articles.title: Representation of environmental issues: Is there a link between campaign and legislative behaviour in the European Parliament?
articles.abstract: This article assesses the link between Members of the European Parliament's campaign salience and legislative behaviour, focusing on environmental issues. Environmental issues were discussed by several MEP candidates during the 2019 campaign and they were important for voters. Nonetheless, it is unclear whether MEPs were consistent with their campaign commitments in their parliamentary votes. MEPs’ environmental salience is computed by coding 50,393 campaign tweets and their legislative behaviour is assessed by examining roll-call votes on amendments related to emissions reduction. Results indicate that MEPs who focused more on environmental issues during the campaign cast more pro-environmental votes. This indicates that the European Parliament can exercise its representative role in domains relevant for EU policy.

articles.title: Bridging innovation and investment: the Paris Agreement’s effect on green and brown US-listed energy stocks
Discourses on the roots and resilience of climate misinformation: perspectives from the Canadian agri-food sector
Sustainable finance taxonomies – Designed to support the transition to a net-zero economy?

articles.title: Offshore finance as statecraft: unpacking the strategic use of OFCs by Chinese capital
articles.authors: Ronen Palan, Ricardo Soares de Oliveira, Yuan Wang, Xinyi Wei
articles.abstract: Nearly three-quarters of Chinese outward foreign direct investment (OFDI) is routed through offshore financial centers (OFCs), a proportion significantly higher than that observed for most Western multinationals. Offshore finance is typically understood as a mechanism of market escape and sovereignty erosion. This article offers an alternative interpretation. Drawing on corporate-level ownership reconstruction and interviews, and focusing on Chinese investment in Africa, we show that offshore structures form part of a differentiated architecture through which Chinese capital is organized and projected internationally. Hong Kong performs a pivotal upstream function, providing globally legible corporate forms that facilitate access to international capital while buffering mainland regulatory constraints. Yet Hong Kong alone does not account for observed patterns. Chinese firms—state-owned and private—layer additional jurisdictions such as the British Virgin Islands, the Cayman Islands, and Singapore into their corporate chains, each serving distinct governance, financing, and risk-management functions. We argue that offshore operates simultaneously as a mechanism of sovereign outsourcing and as a technology of regulatory arbitrage, positioning it as a governance infrastructure embedded within contemporary global capitalism.

articles.title: Trump, the International Criminal Court, and the Future of Global Impunity
articles.abstract: The US has traditionally played a key role in fighting global impunity for atrocity crimes, but the policies of Donald Trump’s administration suggest that a dramatic shift in American priorities may be underway. This article examines America’s commitment to addressing impunity in the context of US relations with the International Criminal Court (ICC). The Trump presidency, I argue, showcases a curious mix of continuity and change in America’s relationship with one of the world’s most prominent international institutions. In particular, Trump’s general strategic approach to the ICC represents continuity with past American presidents, but the brazenness of the specific tactics Trump has used to oppose the ICC represents a notable change. The reverberations of recent American attacks on the ICC raise implications for the future of global impunity that will be felt in three distinct areas: in the US–ICC relationship, among ICC adversaries, and among ICC allies.

articles.title: The Autonomy Paradox: Artificial Intelligence and the Foundations of Political Behavior
articles.abstract: Decades of research in political behavior show that citizens struggle with information, rely on cognitive shortcuts, and face barriers to participation. They are increasingly using AI tools to make sense of political information and express views, while interacting with platform curation systems that shape how views circulate through democratic politics. Although these tools appear suited to address the limits of democratic citizenship, they do more than transmit content. They help interpret information, articulate views, and affect what is prioritized, seen, and circulated. In doing so, these systems shape the formation of political judgments and citizens’ capacity to translate them into action. As a result, they can reduce barriers to participation while weakening the independence of political judgment, or they can support reflective preference formation while constraining citizens’ ability to act on those preferences effectively. We call this tension the autonomy paradox. To make sense of it, we focus on how citizens engage with AI systems in ways that affect belief formation and political action. We develop a framework and research agenda for identifying when AI supports autonomous citizenship, when it substitutes for citizens’ judgment or agency, and why the same systems produce different outcomes across political tasks depending on how citizens use them.

articles.title: Good Governance as Responsible Sovereignty: Francis Deng and the Conflict–Development Nexus
articles.abstract: The South Sudanese UN official, diplomat, and scholar Francis Deng is widely recognized for his intellectual contributions to the Responsibility to Protect (R2P) principle, most notably through his 1996 coauthored publication, Sovereignty as Responsibility: Conflict Management in Africa. However, existing scholarship has paid limited attention to how Deng conceptualized the subject of responsible sovereignty: good governance. Through a situated intellectual history, this article reconstructs Deng’s conception of good governance, exploring its reception before and beyond R2P. I contend that Deng reformulated good governance as primarily concerning conflict management. Deng’s thought and advocacy in the late 1990s then shaped the expansion of the good governance agenda, the rise of human security, and the synchronization of humanitarian and development activities through efforts to bridge the so-called relief–development gap. Hence, I portray Deng as a novel theorist and practitioner of the conflict–development nexus, who sought to enlist the international financial institutions for conflict management, prevention, and resolution prerogatives. In so doing, this article destabilizes existing grand narratives of the post–Cold War international order that hinge on end of history triumphalism and neoliberal ideological diffusion.

content.journal_name: Journal of the European Economic Association

articles.title: When It Hurts the Most: Timing of Parental Job Loss and a Child’s Education,
articles.authors: Paul Bingley, Lorenzo Cappellari, Marco Ovidi
articles.abstract: We estimate how the timing of parental job loss shapes children’s human capital by exploiting plant closures in Danish administrative data. We match treated children to observably similar untreated peers and difference out age-invariant selection using children whose parents are displaced after school completion. Job loss during infancy (ages 0–1) reduces ninth-grade mathematics achievement by 0.04 standard deviations and raises non-completion by one percentage point. Effects are smaller in later childhood. Treated infants are 1.4 percentage points less likely to enrol in general upper-secondary programs. We find that liquidity-constrained families drive these results, suggesting that transient income shocks create permanent educational scars.

articles.title: How Do Households Respond to Expected Inflation? An Investigation of Transmission Mechanisms,
articles.authors: Janet Hua Jiang, Rupal Kamdar, Kelin Lu, Daniela Puzzello
articles.abstract: We investigate the channels through which inflation expectations affect household spending by conducting surveys featuring hypothetical scenarios involving an increase in inflation expectations. Most households did not adjust their current spending plans, often because they perceived inflation expectations as irrelevant or adhered to a fixed budget. Among those who did adjust, most decreased their spending, primarily due to wealth effects. Few households increased spending as prescribed by the traditional intertemporal substitution channel. We also document that financial conditions, cognitive ability, and subjective mental models—such as stagflationary expectations—help predict spending responses and the mechanisms households cite. Our findings provide insights into the discussion of using inflation expectations as a policy tool and highlight key frictions to incorporate into theoretical models.

articles.title: Influencer Cartels
articles.abstract: Social media influencers account for a growing share of marketing worldwide. We demonstrate the existence of a novel form of market failure in the advertising market: influencer cartels, where groups of influencers collude to increase their advertising revenue by inflating their engagement. Our theoretical model shows that influencer cartels can improve consumer welfare if they expand social media engagement to the target audience, or reduce welfare if they divert engagement to less relevant audiences. Drawing on the model’s insights, we empirically examine influencer cartels using novel datasets and machine learning tools, and derive policy implications.

articles.title: Training and Job-to-Job Mobility with Transfer Fees,
articles.abstract: This study examines the potential impact of introducing a transfer system, similar to that used in professional soccer, into the standard labor market. We develop a toy model highlighting the theoretical properties of transfer fees. We show that, unlike non-compete clauses—which generate a trade-off between training and mobility—transfer fees encourage investment in training while preserving efficient mobility toward more productive firms. As a result, such a system brings the economy closer to the social optimum than laissez-faire. We then construct a life-cycle model featuring endogenous job creation and destruction, on-the-job search, and training. Using data from the French Labor Force Survey, we estimate the model’s parameters and conduct counterfactual experiments. Our simulations suggest that a time-limited compensation mechanism would significantly increase employment, training access, and welfare.

articles.title: Organizational Capacity and Project Dynamics,
articles.abstract: Organizational capacity is widely considered central to whether managers or politicians can deliver complex projects in an efficient manner. Yet in practice performance can depend on the interaction of capacity with a host of factors such as political opposition or regulatory constraints. We develop a dynamic theory of project development that examines these interactions. In the model, higher capacity enables faster progress toward completion, but opposing interests may incur costly delays by attempting to revise the distribution of project payoffs. Project designers can avoid revisions by equalizing distributive benefits or inflating project scales to make delays prohibitively costly. We show that welfare is minimized when both capacity and the ability to revise are moderate. More efficient outcomes are either smaller than socially optimal or have highly unequal distributive outcomes.

content.journal_name: Annual Review of Environment and Resources

articles.title: The Past, Present, and Future of Online Biodiversity Knowledge Systems
articles.authors: Hilary Kemp, Alena Cierna, Alice Hughes, Antonella Arcangeli, Arnout van Soesbergen, Ayesha Hargey, Charlie Taylor, Charlotte A. Taylor, M. Eugenia Degano, Falko Buschke, Felix Yi Kui Tin, Heli Sihvonen, Lauren Weatherdon, Lera Miles, Nazli Demirel, Nina Bhola, Osgur McDermott Long, P.J. Stephenson, Vincent Blanqué, Yanina Sica, Zuhail Thatey, Neil D. Burgess
articles.abstract: In recent decades, the availability and accessibility of biodiversity data and the profusion of portals, tools, and platforms through which to utilize them have increased rapidly. This reflects the extensive variety of challenges biodiversity data are being used to address and the need to enhance decision-making by different stakeholder groups. Although this has provided unprecedented opportunities for those outside mainstream academia to contribute to and benefit from these resources, it can create confusion in navigating biodiversity data within a highly saturated landscape. We present a new database of 698 global, more than 200 regional, and at least 1,400 national web-based data systems. We then apply both a newly developed typology for online biodiversity data systems and the DPSR+B (drivers, pressure, state, response, benefits) framework to categorize them. We also consider whether target groups are well-defined for these systems. Our analysis shows delivery gaps in systems and data for nature's benefits, agricultural- and wildlife-related supply chains, and specific pressures such as illegal and unsustainable use. Moreover, users’ inability to find the right systems, or interpret them accurately, may lead to poorer conservation outcomes. We make recommendations regarding next-generation online systems that reduce redundancy, lower costs, and improve delivery of information for decision-making.

articles.title: Climate Modeling
articles.abstract: Modeling of the global climate is reviewed through a delineation of different classes of models and different cultures of use. Climate models are classified on the basis of their degrees of freedom and the extent to which these are simulated—calculated based on first principles—or modeled (usually through gestalt constructs). A new class of computationally intensive models, storm-resolving Earth-system models, is introduced. Their advantages and development challenges are discussed in relation to other classes of models. Artificial intelligence provides a new tool for accessing and enabling interactivity with the information content of these models and may also help harmonize the modeling with data, that is, from impacts, more generally. Two cultures of climate model use are distinguished, one interested in understanding how the climate system works, the other interested in making predictions to inform decisions (future making).

articles.title: Late‐Life Mobility in a Rapidly Ageing Middle‐Income Country: Spatial Patterns and Local Demographic Change in Brazil, 1980–2010
articles.authors: Fernando Antonio Ignacio González, Jean Sleifer
articles.abstract: How do older adults reshape the spatial demography of a middle‐income country undergoing one of the fastest population‐ageing transitions on record? Brazil offers a particularly informative case: its share of population aged 60 or above rose from 6.2% in 1980 to 10.8% in 2010 and is projected to reach 25% by 2050, and a nationally administered pension regime makes benefits fully portable across the country's 5565 municipalities. Using large‐sample microdata from four Brazilian Demographic Censuses (1980–2010, 84 million records harmonised to 4298 stable comparable areas) linked to municipal economic accounts, we document a senior counter‐current with the hallmarks of counter‐urbanisation. Senior inter‐area mobility declines with age yet remains substantial through retirement ages, and it is not local boundary‐hopping: the median senior move covers roughly 100 kilometres and nearly a third crosses state lines. Older Brazilians move against the working‐age tide—the largest metropolitan areas lose retirees on net, while small and medium‐sized interior destinations receive them at rates reaching 5%–6% of initial population per 5‐year window. Receiving areas expand demographically—in total population, working‐age cohorts, employment, housing stock and services activity—but GDP per capita and agricultural value added grow more slowly, a pattern consistent with retirees transmitting purchasing power to destinations whose productive base does not scale with the inflow. These associations are robust to geographic‐amenity controls, pre‐trend conditioning and microregion fixed effects and geographically weighted regressions show they hold across virtually the entire national territory; we are explicit, however, that positive selection of destinations bounds them above any causal effect. We discuss what the Brazilian counter‐current implies for population geography and for other middle‐income countries tracing the same demographic curve.

articles.title: Peer-to-peer accountability and knowledge production in OECD DAC peer reviews
articles.authors: Alice Iannantuoni, Simone Dietrich, Bernhard Reinsberg
articles.abstract: The OECD Development Assistance Committee (DAC) relies on peer reviews to promote accountability in development cooperation. For peer review to function as an accountability mechanism, it must first satisfy a core requirement: peer review evaluations must accurately reflect donor practices. We examine whether DAC peer reviews interpret donor behavior on tied aid in ways that are consistent with observable aid-tying practices and shared DAC standards. Using a newly collected corpus of 143 DAC peer reviews from 1994 to 2020, we find a strong, systematic relationship between the reviewed donor’s aid-tying practices and the resulting content of the review documents. This linkage is driven primarily by explicit recommendations to untie aid and discussions of the standard, rather than by positive recognition of aid tying. Contrary to concerns that peer reviewers may intentionally soften evaluations and criticism to protect their own interests, we find no evidence that reviewers who themselves exhibit higher levels of aid tying produce evaluations that deviate from actual practice. Our findings demonstrate that DAC peer reviews generate credible peer evaluations that strengthen accountability dynamics in development cooperation. These insights contribute to literatures on peer reviews in global governance, the politics of international organizations, and foreign aid.

articles.title: The power of locality: National staff enhance performance in international organizations
articles.authors: Steffen Eckhard, Sebastian Korb, Daniel Baumann
articles.abstract: International organizations (IOs) rely on locally hired staff to translate global mandates into local action, yet the performance implications of localization remain contested. Addressing this gap, this study combines natural language processing (NLP) with a novel dataset of 5,230 project evaluations and staffing information from five United Nations organizations (2007–2022). Building on current research on local staff employment in IO projects together with insights from expert interviews, we test two dominant competing arguments: local capture versus local knowledge. Multilevel and fixed-effects analyses show that projects with higher shares of local staff perform significantly better, but only once local employees constitute at least 60% of the team. The results advance theory on IO effectiveness by shifting attention from local discretion to staff composition, demonstrating that locally embedded knowledge, when institutionally represented in staffing, constitutes a key organizational resource for adaptive implementation.

articles.title: Voting the Same, Feeling Differently: Sister Circles, Black Feminist Epistemologies, and Black Women’s Political Emotions During the Harris Campaign – CORRIGENDUM
articles.authors: Nadia E. Brown, Camille Burge-Hicks, Christine M. Slaughter

articles.title: Bold Claims, Low Wages: Why Voluntary Sustainability Standards ( VSS ) Struggle to Implement Living Wages
articles.abstract: Voluntary sustainability standards (VSS)—such as Fairtrade International and the Forest Stewardship Council—aim to improve sustainability in global supply chains by setting high social and environmental standards and certifying businesses that adopt them. This article examines why some VSS adopt ambitious goals for living wages or living incomes yet continue to certify businesses that only pay a minimum wage. Drawing on previous literature, it offers a typology of five ways that VSS can decouple. Drawing on documents, interviews, and participant observation, it offers detailed case studies of how five VSS have engaged in the coupling and decoupling of wage standards. The research identifies four drivers of decoupling: priorities that complete, costs of coupling, low risk of decoupling, and anticipation that coupling will be easier in the future. It also describes several factors that influence these drivers. Finally, it shows how decoupling may paradoxically facilitate progress, while pressure to fully couple may inhibit transformative change, and concludes with recommendations for avoiding empty claims while harnessing aspirational standards.

articles.title: How considered interests evolve in deliberation: evidence from Swiss citizens’ juries
articles.abstract: Citizens increasingly demand involvement in policymaking, driving the rise of participatory processes like deliberative minipublics. This article introduces a novel longitudinal survey measure to determine the extent to which citizens are more considerate of others’ interests as a result of their participation in such forums. The study explores how participants’ considered interests vary across demographics and process-related factors measured throughout five Swiss minipublics (2019–2023) on different topics and validated using word-embedding techniques on their transcripts. While results show that minipublic participants considered interests different from their own, individuals belonging to less advantaged groups did not consistently show greater consideration of others’ interests. Interest inclusiveness was higher among older individuals, low-income earners and participants in minipublics linked to referendums. This article explains how and why participants in minipublics consider interests beyond their own, which is essential for designing more inclusive participatory processes that engage people from diverse backgrounds in increasingly polarized societies.

articles.title: Who cares about politics under authoritarian rule? Evidence from China
articles.abstract: Departing from mainstream research on political interest in democratic contexts, this study investigates its evolution in an authoritarian setting. To disentangle temporal dynamics, it applies the age–period–cohort interaction model to repeated cross-sectional data from five waves of nationally representative surveys conducted in China. The results demonstrate distinct effects across age, period, and cohort dimensions. Age effects indicate that younger individuals consistently exhibit lower levels of political interest than older adults. Period effects reveal a downward trend in political interest among the Chinese public between 2002 and 2019. Importantly, cohort effects suggest that, contrary to the linear evolutionary predictions of modernization theory, individuals who underwent political socialization during critical historical periods—such as the Great Famine and its aftermath (1959–1963) and the late Cultural Revolution (1974–1978)—as well as those born in the late 1970s and throughout the 1980s, exhibit heightened political interest. These findings contribute to theoretical reflections on the evolution of political interest.
