articles.title: Anti-Elitism Gets the Views: Populist Communication and Popularity on German Political YouTube
articles.abstract: YouTube has become a central venue for political communication, but systematic evidence of how parties employ the platform remains limited. This article examines how German political parties use YouTube and how populist rhetoric shapes engagement. We distinguish between anti-elitism and people-centrism and analyze their prevalence in party videos alongside their effects on video performance. We compile a dataset of official YouTube channels from all major German parties (2017–2025), apply automated transcription, and use a transformer-based model (PopBERT) to detect populist language. Video performance is assessed primarily through views, modeled with quantile regression and hurdle approaches to capture the likelihood of videos reaching the top tier and conditional effects among successful content. Our results show that the Alternative for Germany (AfD) far surpasses other parties in subscribers, video production, and engagement. Content analysis reveals that AfD channels contain markedly higher levels of anti-elitist rhetoric, while people-centrism appears more evenly distributed across the party spectrum. Quantile regression models show that anti-elitism is positively associated with engagement in the upper tail of the view distribution for all parties except the Free Democratic Party (FDP). Hurdle models further indicate that anti-elitism is associated with a higher probability of entering the top performance tier not only for the AfD but also for the Christian Democratic Union / Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU), Left, and the Social Democratic Party (SPD). Results for people-centrism are weaker and less consistent. The study contributes to research on digital populism by showing that anti-elitist rhetoric, more than people-centrism, is associated with video success on YouTube across populist and nonpopulist parties.

articles.title: India's Agricultural Policy Transitions
articles.authors: Avinash Kishore, Bharat Ramaswami, Devesh Roy
articles.abstract: This review traces the evolution of India's agricultural policy regime, centered on price supports, input subsidies, and complex trade policies that oscillate between protectionism and implicit taxation of farmers. It highlights three interlinked challenges: low farm incomes, poor diet quality, and environmental degradation. The policy architecture that ensures food security constrains the pace of agricultural transformation. Reform requires repurposing subsidies and restoring credibility to trade policy. While the digital infrastructure is in place to begin the shift to smarter subsidies, the political path is risky, as policy must seek credible ways to signal protection of farmer interests. Despite these policy rigidities, economic growth and urbanization continue to drive structural changes in agriculture. Diversification away from cereals, new food value chains, and rising integration with nonfarm employment are the key dynamic forces shaping agricultural outcomes. Future outcomes will depend on policy responses to emerging food value chains and new agricultural technologies.

articles.title: Framing Extremist Narratives: A Multi‐Stage Computational Analysis of Discourse Structures, Emotional Mobilization, and Cross‐Platform Migration
articles.authors: Xiaotian Hou, Xiaohan Liu, Mingyu Liu
articles.abstract: Online extremism poses a particularly difficult governance challenge when radical actors adapt and spread grievance, authority, enemy, and recruitment narratives across heterogeneous platforms. This study develops a multi‐stage computational framework for analyzing extremist narratives across platforms. Using a corpus of 22,347 English‐language documents from Twitter/X, Telegram, Gab, public web archives, and extremist‐adjacent forums posted between 2020 and 2023, the study integrates topic modeling, frame classification, psycholinguistic and emotion scoring, semantic cross‐platform matching, qualitative validation, and negative‐control checks. The findings identify eight topic clusters, six recurring narrative frames, and a platform‐migration pattern associated with semantic drift and stronger enemy‐focused framing in less‐moderated destination spaces. The results are consistent with a displacement‐and‐intensification mechanism, although they do not establish causal effects of deplatforming or individual radicalization. The study contributes to computational discourse analysis, coordinated platform governance, and frame‐aware counter‐narrative design.

articles.title: How patronage communicates: information campaigns and government responsiveness in China
articles.abstract: How do social relationships among government officials shape information flows within bureaucratic hierarchies? Classic principal–agent theories emphasize information asymmetries as a source of inefficiency, yet we know far less about the actual nature of communication within bureaucracies. We argue that patron–client ties embedded within formal hierarchies play a central role in structuring internal information flows. Lower-level officials with patronage ties to higher-level leaders have incentives to conduct informal information campaigns that signal diligence and competence as a way to compete for political favors. Using newly assembled data from China—including a rare corpus of internal emails between city-level patrons and county-level clients, as well as original datasets on county governments’ public responses to citizen complaints—we find that client counties communicate more frequently with higher-level officials, more often highlight their diligence in addressing complaints, and more actively defend themselves against accusations. However, client and non-client counties perform similarly in how they respond publicly to citizen complaints. These findings reveal how patronage relations can increase upward information flows without impacting public-facing performance. More broadly, these results suggest that communication in nondemocratic settings may serve to strengthen informal political ties.

articles.title: Policymaking activities of caretaker governments in Western Europe
articles.abstract: In parliamentary democracies, coalition government formation often takes a certain amount of time, during which the outgoing incumbent government remains in office as the “caretaker” until the new government can be formed. While the literature has reached a consensus that caretaker governments retain the policy status quo, empirical evidence remains limited. This article uses original data on government bills from 238 cabinets in 11 Western European countries as descriptive evidence to challenge this long-standing assumption. I propose a timeframe-based, political definition of the caretaking period within the coalition lifecycle and discuss the normative issues with its presence. The over-generalization of the prevalent policy status quo assumption raises critical issues concerning practical caretaking rules, as well as coalition governance and bargaining.

articles.title: Racialization of the democratic peace in foundational embedding models
articles.abstract: One of the most prominent theories in modern international relations is the democratic peace theory, which posits that democracies tend not to engage in armed conflicts with fellow democracies. Recently, Rathbun, Parker, and Pomeroy examined this effect at a microstructural level, performing surveys, computational studies, and meta-analysis. Of particular originality in their work was embedding analysis, which I review and offer a systematic critique of. Then, I propose a new and improved methodology that addresses its issues while leveraging foundational embedding models. My replication results agree with their findings that the democratic peace effect is racialized, that is, it is associated with racial and ethnocentric motivations. The findings offer a timely guide in conducting embedding analysis in political science research.

articles.title: A multilingual, multi-country dataset on gardening and biodiversity awareness across Central and Eastern Europe
articles.authors: Zsófia Varga-Szilay, Lucija Šerić Jelaska, Silva Vilumets, Arvīds Barševskis, Klára Benedek, Danilo Bevk, Agata Jojczyk, Anton Krištín, Jana Růžičková, Eve Veromann, Kinga Gabriela Fetykó, Gergely Szövényi, Gábor Pozsgai
articles.abstract: We present a multi-country and multilingual dataset on garden characteristics, gardening practices, and gardeners’ environmental attitudes based on a questionnaire survey conducted across nine Central and Eastern European countries: Croatia, Czechia, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Poland, Romania, Slovakia, and Slovenia. The survey was collaboratively designed and translated into ten languages by native speakers to ensure cultural and linguistic accuracy. It was distributed online through diverse channels, yielding 5511 responses. The dataset enables exploration of relationships between gardening practices and socio-cultural factors at local, national, and regional scales. The questionnaire covered topics such as garden characteristics, management practices, pesticide use, biodiversity-supporting actions, and environmental awareness, offering a comprehensive overview of gardening in the region. The dataset is suitable for cross-country comparisons, machine learning analyses, and the development of indices that quantify ecological value or management intensity. The multilingual questionnaire supports reuse in future studies, facilitating replication or adaptation elsewhere. By making the dataset openly available, we provide a resource for researchers and practitioners interested in urban biodiversity, sustainability, and human–nature interactions.

articles.title: Origin, gender and academic age diversity indicators for UK research communities
articles.abstract: This paper describes a dataset of community-level diversity indicators for origin, gender and academic age across research communities in UK higher education institutions. The indicators were constructed from individual-level bibliometric metadata for 535,456 research-active individuals in OpenAlex, using onomastic inference for gender and country of origin and publication histories for academic age, with confidence-based filtering to manage inference uncertainty. The unit of analysis is the institution–Unit of Assessment pair defined by the UK Research Excellence Framework (REF) 2021, and the resulting REF 2021-Diversity dataset comprises 1,848 records across 155 institutions and 34 Units of Assessment. The indicators range from simple compositional statistics through standard entropy-based indices to multidimensional Leinster–Cobbold indices to accommodate various use cases and assumptions. The dataset can support benchmarking of research community composition, methodological comparison of diversity measures, and cautiously specified association analyses between community-level diversity indicators and REF-linked quality profiles.

articles.title: From the courtroom to the public: Judicial influence on People’s attitudes toward same-sex marriage in Japan
articles.authors: Robert Nordström, Sou Shinomoto, Antonio Benasaglio Berlucchi
articles.abstract: Can judicial action change public attitudes? While most empirical studies on the societal impact of court rulings have focused on the United States, particularly its Supreme Court, the influence of courts in other contexts remains largely unexplored. This study examines Japan—the only G7 country that does not legally recognize same-sex marriage—and explores how judicial rulings on same-sex marriage influence public attitudes. Using data from an original survey incorporating natural and experimental treatments, the analysis finds that while a court decision has no significant effect in a natural environment, experimental exposure to a reminder of the ruling can shift respondents’ views. The findings suggest that judicial action on same-sex marriage may have limited but measurable impacts on public attitudes, even in unconventional settings, and therefore contribute to discussions of external validity regarding the societal influence of courts.

articles.title: Revisiting the Communication Mediation Model in the Age of Social Media: Longitudinal Evidence From Climate Misinformation Responses in China
articles.authors: Liang Chen, Xiaoming Liu, Lunrui Fu
articles.abstract: The Communication Mediation Model (CMM) posits that media attention stimulates interpersonal discussion, which shapes attitudes and behaviors. Yet its assumptions of linear sequencing and universal applicability remain underexamined. In the era of social media, communication flows are increasingly reciprocal and socially embedded, and response behaviors such as misinformation correction and fact-checking represent new forms of media engagement rather than merely offline actions. Using a three-wave panel survey in China ( n = 499), this study revises the CMM in the context of climate change misinformation on social media by testing temporal pathways and audience heterogeneity. Results show that media attention stimulates interpersonal discussion, which in turn predicts correction, though these relationships unfold concurrently within a single time interval rather than following a staggered temporal order. Multigroup analysis reveals that public self-consciousness conditions pathway activation. Findings highlight how social media environments extend the behavioral scope of the CMM and complicate its assumed temporal order. Theoretical and practical implications are discussed.

articles.title: Scaling Down: Notes From the Laundry Room
articles.abstract: This essay tells the story of a personal experiment in deploying a “deliberative technology” called Polis to start a conversation about the norms of my apartment building’s shared laundry room—a small, quasi-public space ordinarily governed mostly by unspoken rules. The Polis conversation drew meaningful engagement from neighbors, who both voted on shared norms for the space and suggested concrete (and ultimately effective) ways to improve it. Reflecting on this example, I argue that beyond their familiar promise of “scaling up” deliberation, tools like Polis can also facilitate “scaling down,” making it feasible to convene conversations and build a sense of shared interest even in small-scale, everyday settings like the apartment laundry room.

articles.title: Anthropomorphizing AI: Perceptions, Interpretations, and the Humanization of Generative AI
articles.authors: Mohammad Hossein Jarrahi, Amir Karami, Lisa Park, Ensieh Jarrahi, Christoph Lutz
articles.abstract: The rise of generative artificial intelligence (AI), particularly advanced AI chatbots such as ChatGPT, has transformed human–AI interactions by providing unprecedentedly natural interaction environments. These developments have significantly heightened user perceptions of AI as human-like, making anthropomorphism, a tendency to attribute human traits to non-humans, increasingly prevalent. Despite the recognition of the rising anthropomorphism in these interaction modalities, little is known about how people anthropomorphize generative AI, especially in social media discourse. Using Twitter/X as a discursive space, we systematically analyze how users described and engaged with ChatGPT, identifying distinct categories and recurring forms of anthropomorphism. Findings reveal diverse anthropomorphic perceptions, including personification, emotional attributions, cognitive and human-like attributes, social interactions, and human-like personality traits. Building on the observation that social media platforms not only reflect but also actively shape and reinforce anthropomorphic narratives, this study raises important implications for trust, misinformation, user expectations, and human–AI interactions.

articles.title: Unpacking the Relationship Between Algorithmic Literacy and Misinformation: A Multidimensional Approach Using Two Sequential Studies
articles.authors: Teresa Correa, Sebastián Valenzuela, Ingrid Bachmann, Nicolás Tobar Jorquera, Natalia Solís-Valdés, Isabel Pavez
articles.abstract: Digital literacy is often proposed as a remedy for misinformation, yet empirical evidence regarding its effectiveness remains mixed. One reason for these inconsistencies lies in the multidimensional nature of both literacy and misinformation. This article focuses on algorithmic literacy, a distinct and increasingly central form of digital literacy in platform-mediated communication, and examines how its cognitive and behavioral dimensions relate to multiple facets of misinformation engagement. Drawing on two probabilistic survey studies conducted in Chile—a nationally representative face-to-face survey ( N = 1,200) and a random-digit-dial telephone survey of urban adults ( N = 2,265)—we analyze how cognitive (algorithmic awareness and knowledge) and behavioral (strategic actions to navigate algorithmic systems) dimensions of algorithmic literacy relate to perceived misinformation exposure, misinformation sharing, objective and subjective news knowledge, and knowledge miscalibration. Across both studies, a consistent pattern emerges: algorithmic literacy is more strongly associated with cognitive outcomes—especially perceived misinformation exposure and knowledge—than with behavioral outcomes like sharing. Higher algorithmic awareness consistently predicts greater perceived exposure, suggesting heightened recognition, while its link to sharing behavior is less consistent. These studies highlight the relevance of distinguishing cognitive from behavioral dimensions of literacy across different stages of misinformation engagement.

articles.title: “Hearing My People, but Not Seeing My People”: Boundaries of Blackness on TikTok
articles.abstract: Social media is a valuable tool that enables Black individuals to contest their racialized experiences and engage in counterpublic discourse. Importantly, this opens up cultural property and closed conversations to out-group visibility and appropriation. With this in mind, I ask: How do Black social media users engage in boundary work on TikTok? I create a typology of boundary enforcement on the platform, identifying nine video subtypes, and analyze each subtype using Critical Technocultural Discourse Analysis. The findings suggest that Black TikTok users employ various discursive strategies to maintain group boundaries. This study explores how new technologies may impact racialized experiences and identity formation.

articles.title: Policing Queer and Racialized Identities: An Intersectional Approach to Study Police Bias
articles.abstract: Queer people in the United States have been historically over-policed, in a long-standing history of criminalization and oppression by law enforcement. Despite scholars having extensively used administrative records of police stops to uncover racial disparities and bias in law enforcement practices, virtually no studies exist doing the same to examine the discriminatory policing of queerness—by itself, and in the intersection with race. In this article, I fill this gap by analyzing administrative records of ∼3,100,000 stops in the United States between 2018 and 2025, looking at whether civilians perceived as LGBTQ+ are disproportionately targeted by the police in post-stop decisions. Through multiple tests, I find consistent evidence that being queer is associated with a higher probability of being searched, arrested, and be victims of police use of force. Then, using an intersectional approach, I test whether the interaction of race with queerness worsens police discrimination. Results show that bias gets worse for racial minorities who are also LGBTQ+, indicating that a dynamic of intersectional, double disadvantage can be found in police discrimination. This research underscores the importance of applying an intersectional framework to police studies, and the ongoing role of policing in reproducing the marginalization of historically oppressed communities.

articles.title: More Inclusive, Less Attentive: How Digital Intermediaries Expand News Audiences but Facilitate Inequalities in News Attentiveness
Migration information campaigns as bureaucratic performances: governing through visibility
articles.abstract: Drawing on a mixed-methods analysis of 97 migration information campaigns implemented across Europe between 2019 and 2026 and more than thirty interviews with migration governance practitioners, policymakers, and international organization staff, this article reconceptualizes migration information campaigns as bureaucratic performances. Rather than informing migrants, campaigns operate as visible governance outputs through which states, international organizations, and implementing agencies stage action, secure legitimacy, and reproduce migration governance systems. The analysis shows that migration information campaigns have become routinized instruments of migration governance whose design is structured around risk framing and strategic ambiguity, and whose primary audiences are often institutional rather than migrant populations. Across governance contexts, campaigns perform distinct functions: signaling cooperation in countries of origin, demonstrating compliance in transit settings, and projecting responsiveness in destination countries. The article argues that migration information campaigns persist not because they influence migration decisions, but because they are institutionally useful. Their value lies in producing visibility, legitimacy, and auditable evidence of action in contexts where governing migration outcomes is difficult. In doing so, the article challenges dominant evaluative approaches in migration studies by showing that policy instruments may endure even when they are widely acknowledged to have uncertain or limited behavioural effects. Migration information campaigns, it concludes, are not failed interventions; they are successful performances of governance.

articles.title: Assessing pedestrian responses to autonomous and personal mobility robots in crowded public spaces
articles.authors: Dominik Wojcikiewicz, Aude Billard, Diego Paez-Granados
articles.abstract: Robots increasingly share spaces with people, supporting delivery services and mobility for the aging populations, yet their ability to share space comfortably lacks understanding and benchmarks for designers and policy-makers. We compared human-robot (HRI) and human-human (HHI) interactions across four real-world crowd datasets spanning Europe, North America, and Asia, using a unified pipeline to detect interactions, stratify by crowd density, and model pedestrian behavior. Local motion patterns (speed, acceleration, and jerk) remained closely matched between HRI and HHI across all densities. In contrast, proxemics diverged, with effects that grew approximately linearly with robot speed and weakened under higher crowding: In the dataset with the faster navigating robot, pedestrians maintained about 0.23 meters more clearance around the robot than around other pedestrians under less crowded conditions and about 0.05 meters more under more crowded conditions, while in the dataset with the predominantly stationary robot, the corresponding differences were small and inconsistent across crowding levels. The main conclusions were robust to parameter variations and remained stable across a broad range of motion-processing and interaction-labeling settings. Our findings provide density- and speed-aware benchmarks for proxemics in social robot navigation and empirically grounded targets for design, evaluation, and modeling across robotics and urban mobility.

articles.title: Escalation dynamics and the severity of wars
articles.authors: Aaron Clauset, Barbara F. Walter, Lars-Erik Cederman, Kristian Skrede Gleditsch
articles.abstract: Although very large wars remain an enduring threat in global politics, we lack a clear understanding of how some wars become large and costly, while most do not. There are three possibilities: Large conflicts begin with intense fighting, accumulate severity over a long duration, or escalate in intensity over time. Using detailed within-conflict data on civil and interstate wars (1946–2008), we show that escalation dynamics—variations in fighting intensity within an armed conflict—are the primary mechanism for producing large conflicts. Civil wars, however, tend to deescalate once they become very large, limiting their overall severity, while interstate wars exhibit a persistent risk of continual escalation. Simple models of within-conflict severity dynamics show that this distinction compactly explains the historical size distributions of civil and interstate wars, and unconditioned escalation is a plausible mechanism for Richardson’s law—the power law pattern in the frequency and severity of interstate conflicts. The dynamics of escalation within conflicts have broad implications for conflict theory and risk assessment.

articles.title: Most people who agree with you won’t protest: Predictors of marches and demonstrations from six decades of research
articles.abstract: Protest and activism are endemic and potent features of many nations’ political life and critical potential counters to democratic backsliding and authoritarianism. In this review article, we meta-analytically examine six decades of research findings on what explains participation, focusing particularly on two well-studied protest forms: marches and demonstrations. Focusing on these iconic and common forms of protest participation ensures accurate research comparison, allowing us to identify sets of variables that are consistently important, others that are not consistently important, and still others that need additional research. Our focus on survey-based studies also allows us to compare research that includes both participants and nonparticipants, which is critical for methodologically sound comparisons. Our analysis of 181 survey-based studies (with more than 1800 different estimates) shows that survey research strongly supports the relevance of political interest, political ideology, membership in organizations, and digital/social media use in explaining participation, as well as demographic variables such as education, age, and living in an urban center. Our review also offers important suggestions for future survey research and micromobilization research more broadly.

articles.title: Individual and differential harm in redistricting
Longitudinal effect of early social media use on standardized learning outcomes during school career
articles.authors: Marco Gui, Chiara Respi, Giovanni Abbiati, Cristiana Paladini, Sofia Ercolanoni, Francesca Milzani, Tiziana Pirola, Giovanni Vezzoli
articles.abstract: This study uses difference-in-differences models to evaluate the impact of early social media use on academic performance among children aged 7–16 years. A dataset comprising 5,227 students from northern Italy was constructed by merging data from a questionnaire on lifetime digital media habits with longitudinal standardized test scores in Italian, English and mathematics. Participants who created a personal social media account in 6th, 7th or 8th grade were separately matched with late adopters who initiated their first social media account in the 9th grade or later. The findings provide compelling evidence that early engagement with social media adversely affects learning outcomes. Additional findings on the effects of early social media use on other academic outcomes for which we do not have longitudinal data are in line with our main findings. We also find supporting evidence that a substantial part of this negative effect is mediated by students’ smartphone pervasiveness in key moments of the day.
